table.header: Method Participants

table.text: Data from 269 participants were analyzed (157 women, 112 men; Mage = 41.1 years, SDage = 12.9, range = 20-75).
table.header: Method Participants

table.text: Participants were asked to imagine that they were in a situation in which it was necessary to solve a math problem and to indicate whether they felt anxious in such situations (a four-point Likert scale; 1 -"I definitely do not feel anxiety", 2 -"I rather do not feel anxiety", 3 -"I rather feel anxiety", 4 -"I definitely feel anxiety").
table.header: Math anxiety

table.text: Participants were asked how anxious they would feel in response to the situation described in each item, and the possible responses were as follows: "not at all", "a little", "a fair amount", "much", and "very much".
table.header: Spatial anxiety

table.text: Participants were recruited via Prolific and received £6.
table.header: Procedure

table.text: The participants completed the questionnaires in the following order: Cognitive Test Anxiety Scale, Spatial Anxiety Questionnaire, Ten-Item Personality Inventory, Abbreviated Math Anxiety Scale, Math Anxiety Questionnaire for Adults, Single-Item Math Anxiety Scale, State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, and Math achievement problems.
table.header: Procedure

table.text: As participants were informed during recruitment that they would complete questionnaires and solve mathematical tasks, self-selection related to attitudes toward mathematics, anxiety, or competence cannot be ruled out.
table.header: Study limitations and future research directions

table.text: Participant consent statement: All participants were informed about the purpose and procedures of the study and gave their informed consent to participate.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

live_data_statements: Four participants were excluded from the analysis because they failed at least two out of five attention checks.
Data from 269 participants were analyzed (157 women, 112 men; Mage = 41.1 years, SDage = 12.9, range = 20-75).

Participants were asked to imagine that they were in a situation in which it was necessary to solve a math problem and to indicate whether they felt anxious in such situations (a four-point Likert scale; 1 -"I definitely do not feel anxiety", 2 -"I rather do not feel anxiety", 3 -"I rather feel anxiety", 4 -"I definitely feel anxiety").

Participants were asked how anxious they would feel in response to the situation described in each item, and the possible responses were as follows: "not at all", "a little", "a fair amount", "much", and "very much".
Participants were recruited via Prolific and received £6.

The participants completed the questionnaires in the following order: Cognitive Test Anxiety Scale, Spatial Anxiety Questionnaire, Ten-Item Personality Inventory, Abbreviated Math Anxiety Scale, Math Anxiety Questionnaire for Adults, Single-Item Math Anxiety Scale, State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, and Math achievement problems.

As participants were informed during recruitment that they would complete questionnaires and solve mathematical tasks, self-selection related to attitudes toward mathematics, anxiety, or competence cannot be ruled out.
Participant consent statement: All participants were informed about the purpose and procedures of the study and gave their informed consent to participate.

text.text: The gender gap in math anxiety (and in the link between math anxiety and math achievement) is not so salient when other anxieties are controlled for.

Numeracy proficiency and participation in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) are widely recognized as important predictors of higher earnings and better financial and health decisions (Black et al., 2021; OECD, 2016 OECD, , 2024)).
text.formatted: Numeracy proficiency and participation in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) are widely recognized as important predictors of higher earnings and better financial and health decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Black et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">OECD, 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">OECD, , 2024))</ref>.

text.text: For this reason, numerous initiatives have been undertaken worldwide to strengthen students' math achievement at all stages of education.
However, the effectiveness of these efforts may depend not only on interventions aimed at improving math achievement, but also on efforts addressing the determinants of these skills.

Among the predictors of math achievement, both individual factors (sociodemographic, cognitive, affective, motivational) and environmental factors (family-, school-, peer-related) have been identified (Lau et al., 2022; Luttenberger et al., 2018; Meece et al., 1990; Retanal & Maloney, 2026).
text.formatted: Among the predictors of math achievement, both individual factors (sociodemographic, cognitive, affective, motivational) and environmental factors (family-, school-, peer-related) have been identified <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Lau et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Luttenberger et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Meece et al., 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Retanal & Maloney, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Math anxiety (MA) is one of the most extensively studied and well-established correlates of math achievement (Pelegrina et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Math anxiety (MA) is one of the most extensively studied and well-established correlates of math achievement <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Pelegrina et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: MA is defined as "a feeling of tension and anxiety that interferes with the manipulation of numbers and the solving of mathematical problems in a wide variety of ordinary life and academic situations" (Richardson & Suinn, 1972, p. 551).
text.formatted: MA is defined as "a feeling of tension and anxiety that interferes with the manipulation of numbers and the solving of mathematical problems in a wide variety of ordinary life and academic situations" <ref type="bibr">(Richardson & Suinn, 1972, p. 551)</ref>.

text.text: In line with this definition, MA is a multidimensional construct encompassing anxiety related to learning, testing, and problem solving, with these dimensions strongly interrelated and also reflected in general feelings toward mathematics (Dowker et al., 2016; Hart & Ganley, 2019; Hopko et al., 2003).

text.text: MA is typically understood and assessed as a trait (Orbach et al., 2019), and this is the approach we adopt in the present study.

text.text: MA develops gradually from childhood, peaks in adolescence, and persists into adulthood, even after the end of formal education (Hart & Ganley, 2019; Hembree, 1990).

text.text: This persistence may be important for the transfer of MA to subsequent generations, as previous research indicates that parental and teachers' MA is associated with children's MA and their mathematics achievement (Beilock et al., 2010; Maloney et al., 2015; Ramirez et al., 2018b).

text.text: MA has attracted considerable attention because most studies involving children, adolescents, and adults suggest that girls and women report higher levels of this anxiety (Eidlin-Levy et al., 2023), which may be linked to lower female participation in STEM fields (Lunardon et al., 2022; Megreya et al., 2025).

text.text: Previous research suggests that reducing MA may enhance math achievement and participation in STEM, particularly among women (Ramirez et al., 2018a).
text.formatted: Previous research suggests that reducing MA may enhance math achievement and participation in STEM, particularly among women <ref type="bibr">(Ramirez et al., 2018a)</ref>.

text.text: However, planning effective interventions requires a deeper understanding of the factors associated with gender differences in MA.

The present study aims to investigate the factors that mediate the relationship between gender and MA and to examine whether gender differences exist in the association between MA and math achievement.
To address these aims, we additionally analyze the correlates of MA and gender differences in these correlates.

To better understand the mechanisms underlying gender differences in MA, it is essential to examine the correlates of MA, which have themselves been widely investigated with regard to gender differences.

Research on the specificity of MA has been extensive, and findings indicate that it is a distinct form of anxiety that is related to, but not reducible to, neuroticism (Lunardon et al., 2022), general (Malanchini et al., 2017), test (Caviola et al., 2022), or spatial anxiety (Delage et al., 2022; Sokolowski et al., 2019).

text.text: Although all types of anxiety can be analyzed both as stable traits and as situational states, here we focus on traitlevel constructs.
Math achievement is another key correlate of MA that is conceptually distinct from anxiety and has been extensively investigated (Barroso et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2019).

text.text: Neuroticism Neuroticism (the inverse of emotional stability) is a broad personality trait reflecting a stable tendency to experience negative affect, emotional reactivity, and difficulty regulating distress across situations (Gosling et al., 2003).

text.text: Individuals low in emotional stability tend to be more sensitive to stressors and more prone to experiencing worry, tension, and mood fluctuations.

Previous studies indicate that neuroticism is positively and weakly-to-moderately related to MA (e.g., r = .32, Lunardon et al., 2022), likely acting as its precursor by increasing the likelihood that mathematics-related situations are appraised as threatening and by amplifying worry and emotional reactivity during mathematical problem solving.

text.text: Women tend to report higher levels of neuroticism than men (Chapman et al., 2007; Lunardon et al., 2022), which may partially explain gender differences in MA, as greater emotional reactivity and worry in women may increase vulnerability to anxiety in mathematics-related contexts.

text.text: General anxiety is conceptualized as a stable disposition to experience worry and tension across a wide range of situations (Spielberger, 1983).

text.text: Individuals high in general anxiety tend to perceive ambiguous or demanding situations as more threatening and to respond with elevated and persistent worry.

Although general anxiety and neuroticism originate from different theoretical traditions, they are conceptually similar in that both capture relatively stable individual differences in emotional vulnerability that may predispose individuals to higher levels of MA.
Consistent with this view, previous research indicates substantial statistical overlap between general anxiety and neuroticism (e.g., r > .70; Jylhä & Isometsä, 2006).

text.text: Therefore, in the present paper, we treat both constructs as manifestations of trait anxiety vulnerability.

text.text: Many mathematical tasks rely on spatial representations and transformations, making anxiety experienced during spatial processing particularly likely to generalize to mathematics.

Despite sharing a common negative valence, neuroticism, general anxiety, test anxiety, and spatial anxiety differ in their degree of conceptual overlap: neuroticism and general anxiety show the greatest overlap, whereas test anxiety and spatial anxiety are more domain-specific and overlap to a lesser extent.

Accordingly, each construct is expected to account for a unique proportion of the variance in gender differences in MA, with the exception that, due to their substantial overlap, neuroticism and general anxiety should not be included simultaneously in the same analyses.

Taking into account the prominent positive associations between spatial ability and math achievement (Mix et al., 2016), and findings that women tend to perform worse on spatial tasks and report higher spatial anxiety than men (Geer et al., 2024), it can be expected that, among various types of anxiety, spatial anxiety particularly contributes to the relationship between gender and MA.

text.text: The inconsistent findings regarding gender differences in the MA-math achievement relationship may partly stem from insufficient control of broader emotional vulnerability factors.

Many studies examining gender moderation have not simultaneously accounted for neuroticism, general anxiety, test anxiety, or spatial anxiety, despite strong theoretical and empirical links between these constructs and MA.

Because girls and women typically report higher levels of several anxiety forms, the observed gender moderation effects may partly reflect shared emotional vulnerability rather than MA-specific mechanisms.

Therefore, simultaneously controlling for multiple anxiety-related constructs appears crucial for clarifying whether gender differences in the MA-math achievement relationship reflect domain-specific MA effects or broader affective dispositions.
This integrative approach may help reconcile inconsistent findings in the literature and provide a more precise estimate of gender-specific MA effects.

Although a substantial body of research has examined MA (Dowker et al., 2016; Hart & Ganley, 2019), important gaps remain regarding the relative contribution of different affective and math achievement-related factors to gender differences in MA in adulthood and to gender differences in the relationship between MA and math achievement.
text.formatted: Although a substantial body of research has examined MA <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Dowker et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Hart & Ganley, 2019)</ref>, important gaps remain regarding the relative contribution of different affective and math achievement-related factors to gender differences in MA in adulthood and to gender differences in the relationship between MA and math achievement.

text.text: In particular, prior studies have rarely considered multiple anxiety constructs simultaneously, despite their partial conceptual overlap and their connections with both gender and MA.

As a result, it remains unclear which factors uniquely contribute to gender differences in MA and in the MA-math achievement relationship, and how much variance in MA can be explained when these constructs are examined jointly.

The present study addresses this gap by adopting an integrative approach that situates anxiety constructs along a hierarchical continuum, from more domain-specific forms of anxiety (spatial and test anxiety), to broader emotional vulnerability (neuroticism and general anxiety), while also including math achievement within a single analytic approach.
This approach is grounded in hierarchical models of anxiety, which posit that more specific anxieties may emerge from broader dispositional vulnerabilities while retaining their domain specificity.

Given the substantial conceptual and empirical overlap between neuroticism and general anxiety, only neuroticism was retained in the joint analyses to avoid redundancy and to more precisely estimate the unique contribution of the remaining predictors.
The study applied a correlational cross-sectional design and examined the proposed mediation mechanism and the covariation between variables.
Although both models are theoretically plausible, they do not constitute evidence of causal effects, allowing alternative explanations.

First, we examine the mediating effects of spatial anxiety in the relationship between gender and MA and then assess the proportion of MA variance explained by gender and spatial anxiety to replicate the most robust prior findings (Delage et al., 2022; Sokolowski et al., 2019).

text.text: Next, we extend the model by adding neuroticism and test anxiety to evaluate their incremental mediation effects and assess the additional variance explained beyond spatial anxiety.
Finally, we include math achievement to determine whether it serves as an additional mediator and accounts for further variance in MA not captured by the affective factors.
Our stepwise strategy allows us to assess both the incremental mediation effects and the cumulative variance explained by the proposed predictors (see Figure 2).

text.text: Then, we examine whether the strength of the relationship between MA and math achievement differs by gender, both before and after controlling for multiple anxiety-related constructs (spatial anxiety, test anxiety, neuroticism).
This analysis is important because previous findings on gender differences have been inconsistent and may reflect insufficient control for broader emotional vulnerability.
Accordingly, we include spatial anxiety, test anxiety, and neuroticism as covariates, given their conceptual and empirical overlap with MA (see Figure 3).

text.text: Taken together, the study aims to answer three research questions: Do various types of anxiety and math achievement mediate the relationship between gender and MA?
What percentage of the variance in MA can be accounted for by gender, various types of anxiety, and math achievement?
Does the relationship between MA and math achievement differ significantly in women and men when various types of anxiety are controlled for?

Regarding the first research question, we expected to replicate the findings of Delage et al. (2022) and Sokolowski et al. (2019), namely that spatial anxiety, particularly in the domains of navigation and manipulation, mediates the relationship between gender and MA.

(2022)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Sokolowski et al. (2019)</ref>, namely that spatial anxiety, particularly in the domains of navigation and manipulation, mediates the relationship between gender and MA.

text.text: We further expect test anxiety to function as an additional significant mediator, given that MA is closely linked to evaluative contexts.
Finally, neuroticism, as a broader disposition reflecting negative emotionality, is expected to play a comparatively less prominent role.
Regarding math achievement, we did not pose a hypothesis due to the contradictory findings of previous studies.
As for the second research question, we expected that models of increasing complexity would account for progressively more variance.

Finally, regarding the third research question, given the inconsistent findings regarding gender differences in the MA-math achievement relationship and the limited number of studies that have simultaneously controlled for multiple anxiety-related constructs, the present study treats this issue as an open empirical question.
Accordingly, we do not formulate a directional hypothesis regarding gender differences in the strength of the association between MA and math achievement.
Instead, we examine whether such differences emerge before and after controlling for broader emotional vulnerability and domain-specific anxieties.
In total, 273 adults residing in the UK with fluent English participated in the online study.
Four participants were excluded from the analysis because they failed at least two out of five attention checks.
Data from 269 participants were analyzed (157 women, 112 men; Mage = 41.1 years, SDage = 12.9, range = 20-75).
Three scales were used to capture the multidimensional nature of MA.

The first was the Abbreviated Math Anxiety Scale (Hopko et al., 2003), consisting of nine items with two subscales: testing MA (α = .88) and learning MA (α = .90), comprising four and five items, respectively.

Participants indicated their level of anxiety in a given situation using a five-point Likert scale (1 -"low anxiety", 5 -"high anxiety").

To capture the multidimensional nature of MA, we created a composite MA score based on all the scales (see Appendix).
Its McDonald's ω for the second-order latent factor was .94.

We quantified spatial anxiety using the Spatial Anxiety Questionnaire (Lyons et al., 2018), consisting of three subscales with eight items each (24 in total): spatial imagery anxiety (SA-I, α = .88), navigation anxiety (SA-N, α = .92), and mental manipulation anxiety (SA-M, α = .96).

text.text: Participants were asked how anxious they would feel in response to the situation described in each item, and the possible responses were as follows: "not at all", "a little", "a fair amount", "much", and "very much".

Example items are as follows: "Asked to give a detailed description of a person's face whom you've only met once" (SA-I), "Memorizing routes and landmarks on a map for an upcoming exam" (SA-N), and "Asked to imagine and mentally rotate a 3-dimensional figure" (SA-M).

Neuroticism was measured using the Ten-Item Personality Inventory (Gosling et al., 2003).

text.text: Although other personality traits were measured, only the neuroticism subscale consisting of two items, i.e., "Anxious, easily upset" and "Calm, emotionally stable" (α = .72), was analyzed.

Participants responded using a seven-point slider (1 -"disagree strongly", 2 -"disagree moderately", 3 -"disagree a little", 4 -"neither agree nor disagree", 5 -"agree a little", 6 -"agree moderately", 7 -"agree strongly").
For interpretative consistency with other anxiety measures, the scale was reverse-scored so that higher scores indicated higher neuroticism.

Because mathematics comprises partially distinct domains, we assessed participants' achievement across core content areas (i.e., arithmetic, algebra, and geometry) to obtain a broad and representative estimate of mathematical competence.
Math achievement was assessed with 20 single-choice math problems, each with five response options (α = .77).
They targeted arithmetic ("600 g of cake costs £8.40.

The study was approved by the Ethics Committee for Research at the Faculty of Philosophy, Jagiellonian University and run online in Qualtrics XM, lasting approximately 30 minutes.
Participants were recruited via Prolific and received £6.
They were informed during recruitment that they would complete questionnaires and solve mathematical tasks.
Each questionnaire was displayed on one screen.
Because all questions were mandatory, there were no missing data.

The participants completed the questionnaires in the following order: Cognitive Test Anxiety Scale, Spatial Anxiety Questionnaire, Ten-Item Personality Inventory, Abbreviated Math Anxiety Scale, Math Anxiety Questionnaire for Adults, Single-Item Math Anxiety Scale, State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, and Math achievement problems.
Finally, participants answered demographic questions and could share their opinions about the study.

text.text: Prior to testing hypotheses, we examined the relevant test assumptions and found no evidence of serious violations.
In the first step, we conducted zero-order Pearson correlation analyses and independentsamples t-tests to examine gender differences in MA, other forms of anxiety, and math achievement.
Then, we addressed the three research questions in two analytic steps.

To address the first and second research questions, we tested three multiple-mediation models in lavaan (Rosseel, 2012), with gender (women = 1, men = 0) as the predictor and the MA composite score as the outcome.

text.text: Model 1 included the three dimensions of spatial anxiety (imagery, navigation, mental manipulation) as mediators.
Model 2 added neuroticism and test anxiety.
Model 3 additionally included math achievement.
The ordering of models allowed us to evaluate both the incremental mediation effects and the additional variance in MA explained by progressively broader sets of predictors.
In all models, the mediators were allowed to covary, enabling estimation of the unique indirect effect associated with each mediator while accounting for shared variance among mediators.
All three models were just-identified (df = 0); therefore, global SEM fit indices and likelihood-ratio tests of model fit were not informative and are not reported.
The incremental contribution of added mediators is indexed by changes in the variance in MA explained (R²), reported alongside the R² of each mediator.
Indirect effects are reported as unstandardized coefficients (B) with their corresponding BCa confidence intervals; effects whose CIs excluded zero were considered significant.

To address the third research question, which concerns whether the strength of the MAmath achievement relationship differs between women and men, we computed Pearson zeroorder and partial correlations between MA and math achievement separately for women and men.
The partial correlations controlled for spatial imagery anxiety, navigation anxiety, mental manipulation anxiety, neuroticism, and test anxiety.
Gender differences in the magnitude of these correlations were tested using Fisher's z test for two independent correlations.

This analysis treats gender as a moderator of the MA-math achievement association and is conceptually complementary to, but distinct from, the mediation analyses, in which gender is treated as a predictor of MA.

The two strategies address different questions: whereas the mediation models examined whether gender differences in MA could be statistically accounted for by the proposed mediators, the separate correlation analyses for women and men tested whether the association between MA and math achievement differed by gender after controlling for shared variance with the affective variables.
Both analytic approaches were included because the study aimed to examine complementary hypothetical models within a correlational framework.

Our study addressed three research questions in a sample of adults with a wide age range.
First, we found that gender differences in MA are significantly weaker when spatial anxiety, test anxiety, neuroticism, and math achievement are considered as mediators.
Second, we demonstrated that gender, all the aforementioned anxieties, and math achievement together account for 66% of the variance in MA levels.
Third, we found that the strength of the relationship between MA and math achievement in women and men is weaker when other anxieties are controlled for.
Moreover, there are no significant differences between women and men in the strength of the relationship between MA and math achievement, regardless of whether other anxieties are controlled for.

Given the inclusion of multiple affective mediators and math achievement across models, we discuss their mediating roles in the gender-MA relationship sequentially (spatial anxiety, neuroticism and test anxiety, and math achievement).
First, we examined mediation using the domain-specific affective mediators, namely the different dimensions of spatial anxiety.

Previous research (Delage et al., 2022; Sokolowski et al., 2019) has found spatial anxiety to be a robust mediator of gender differences in MA in young adults in the areas of mental manipulation and navigation.

text.text: Notably, contrary to Delage et al. ( 2022), but consistent with Sokolowski et al. (2019), we did not find significant gender differences in spatial imagery anxiety.

text.text: The results indicating that mental manipulation and navigation, but not imagery, mediate gender differences in MA are convincing given that the corresponding Spatial Anxiety Scale subscales primarily tap dynamic spatial transformations and route-planning processes that overlap with mathematical reasoning demands, whereas the imagery subscale focuses mainly on static visual memory and descriptive detail, which are less directly related to mathematics.

Importantly, this pattern is consistent with meta-analyses showing that gender differences are largest in mental rotation, moderate in spatial perception, and small or inconsistent in spatial visualization (Linn & Petersen, 1985; Voyer et al., 1995).

text.text: Research by Lawton (1994) suggests that gender differences in spatial abilities and spatial anxiety may stem from differential reliance on navigation strategies, unequal spatial experience, and sociocultural constraints on environmental exploration among girls, which may help explain inconsistencies across studies regarding gender differences in various dimensions of spatial anxiety.

text.text: Beyond spatial anxiety, high neuroticism may increase the risk of developing MA by heightening threat perception and weakening emotional regulation in math-related situations.
Correspondingly, high level of test anxiety may be associated with MA, as math tasks often evoke fears of failure and negative evaluation.

As studies generally show that these types of anxiety are higher in girls and women than in boys and men (Caviola et al., 2022; Lunardon et al., 2022; Lyons et al., 2018), each can be considered a potential mediator of the relationship between gender and MA.

text.text: Indeed, Szczygieł (2020) found that general anxiety fully mediated gender differences in MA in children.

text.text: Given MA's persistence in adulthood (Hart & Ganley, 2019; Hembree, 1990), a similar pattern could be expected in adults.

text.text: However, our results do not support the mediating role of neuroticism or test anxiety in the relationship between gender and MA, when spatial anxiety (and math achievement) are controlled for, or not.
Although gender predicted neuroticism, its indirect effect on MA was weak and non-significant.
Test anxiety significantly predicted MA but was not significantly related to gender, ruling it out as a mediator.

Thus, while affective factors are associated with MA overall, they are not so important in accounting for gender differences in adults when different types of spatial anxiety (and math achievement) are controlled for.

Therefore, gender differences in MA in adults are more strongly related to differences between women and men in emotions associated with spatial navigation and mental manipulation than to gender differences in neuroticism and test anxiety.

This pattern suggests that, whereas in childhood general anxiety may account for much of the gender differences in MA (Szczygieł, 2020), in adulthood more domain-specific anxieties, likely shaped through educational experience, appear to be more closely linked to MA.

Previous research findings on the gender gap in math achievement are inconclusive (Kaiser & Zhu, 2022), however, if such gender differences are observed, they may contribute to higher levels of MA in women than in men.

text.text: Finally, we investigated what percentage of the variance in MA can be accounted for by gender, various types of anxiety, and math achievement.
We found that gender and spatial anxiety accounted for 48% of the variance in MA, which increased to 56% with the addition of neuroticism and test anxiety.
When math achievement was added, the total explained variance in MA rose to 66%.
These results are consistent with Sokolowski et al. (2019), who found that gender, spatial anxiety, and perceived and observed spatial manipulation abilities accounted for 65% of MA variance.

text.text: Although the full model explained a substantial proportion of variance in MA (66%), the unique contribution of gender was relatively modest (5%).
This suggests that gender is best conceptualized as a distal correlate whose association with MA is largely accounted for by correlated affective traits and math achievement.
Accordingly, the conclusions regarding gender effects should be interpreted as relatively small in magnitude.
We conclude that gender, spatial anxiety, more general types of anxiety, and math achievement are key factors determining the level of MA in adults.

However, we refrain from concluding that spatial anxiety is uniquely central (accounting for nearly 50% of variance in MA in our models), as we did not test alternative model specifications (e.g., models progressing from more general to more domain-specific forms of anxiety), and given the substantial intercorrelations among the examined variables.

The remaining variance is likely explained by cognitive and environmental factors (Justicia-Galiano et al., 2023; Lau et al., 2022; Retanal & Maloney, 2026; Szczygieł et al., 2024 Szczygieł et al., , 2025)).

text.text: Gender differences in the strength of the relationship between MA and math achievement were not significant, regardless of whether other anxieties were controlled for.

This pattern is consistent with several prior studies reporting comparable MA-achievement associations in women and men (e.g., Hill et al., 2016; Reali et al., 2016), although it contrasts with research suggesting stronger links in women (e.g., Yu et al., 2024) or in first-grade primary school boys (Szczygieł, 2020).

text.text: The present findings contribute to the mixed literature by suggesting that previously reported gender moderation effects may partly reflect insufficient control for broader affective factors.

Because girls and women tend to report higher levels of several forms of anxiety, gender differences in the MA-math achievement relationship observed in some studies may, in part, capture shared emotional vulnerability rather than MA-specific processes.
At the same time, the broader literature suggests that the magnitude of gender differences in the MA-math achievement relationship may depend on developmental stage and sociocultural context.

For example, some evidence from younger samples indicates stronger associations in boys (Szczygieł, 2020), whereas cross-cultural work has reported stronger links in girls in certain educational contexts (Yu et al., 2024).

text.text: These inconsistencies may reflect differences in stereotype exposure, evaluative pressure, or educational experiences across age groups and cultures.
Future longitudinal and cross-cultural research is therefore needed to clarify when and under what conditions gender differences in the MA-math achievement relationship emerge.
The study's limitations are as follows.
The design was correlational and cross-sectional; therefore, the mediation models should not be interpreted as evidence of causal mechanisms or temporal ordering.
Although we focused on traits, that is, relatively stable individual differences, alternative model specifications remain theoretically plausible.
Future research should use longitudinal designs (and, where feasible, intervention paradigms) to establish temporal precedence and to better distinguish between competing directional accounts.

Because the mediation models were just-identified/saturated and differed in the set of observed variables included, they could not be formally compared using global SEM fit indices or likelihood-ratio tests for nested models.
Therefore, conclusions about the incremental contribution of added mediators are based on changes in explained variance rather than on formal SEM model-fit comparisons.
In our study, the task order was fixed.
As we used a correlational design and measured traits, this should not have confounded the results.
Nevertheless, future studies should counterbalance the task order.
We should also note that the sample included more women than men.
This imbalance likely reflects typical self-selection patterns in voluntary psychological research, but it may also indicate differential willingness to participate in a study involving mathematics.

As participants were informed during recruitment that they would complete questionnaires and solve mathematical tasks, self-selection related to attitudes toward mathematics, anxiety, or competence cannot be ruled out.
Importantly, anxiety-related constructs in our models are conceptually and statistically overlapping.
To reduce redundancy, we did not include state anxiety in the analyses.
Nevertheless, future work could explicitly model a higher-order negative affectivity factor and examine whether domain-specific pathways persist after accounting for this shared variance.

text.text: Given established links between spatial processing and mathematics, future research should include both spatial performance measures and spatial anxiety to clarify their relative and joint contributions to MA and math achievement.
Additionally, these studies and ours differed in the method used to measure math achievement.

Future studies should employ both time-pressured arithmetic tasks and broader sets of math problems to be solved without time pressure, to investigate potential task dependence underlying inconsistent findings.

text.text: Finally, it should be noted that gender differences in self-reported anxiety that we found may partly reflect differences in the social acceptability of emotional expression.
Women may be more willing to acknowledge and report anxiety symptoms, whereas men may be less likely to disclose such experiences due to gender-related social expectations (McLean & Anderson, 2009).

text.text: Our study supports previous findings regarding the gender gap in MA, but these differences appear to be weaker when spatial anxiety, test anxiety, neuroticism, and math achievement are accounted for.
We conclude that gender differences in MA are largely statistically indirect and can be substantially accounted for by associated affective factors and math achievement.
We suggest that interventions aimed at reducing spatial anxiety in the domains of mental manipulation and navigation in women could help reduce the gender gap in MA.

The remaining indirect paths, including test anxiety and neuroticism, were nonsignificant, suggesting that spatial anxiety in navigation and manipulation plays a key role in accounting for gender differences in MA, likely because both types are related to mathematics.

Finally, the relationship between MA and math achievement, tested separately in women and men, is weaker when controlling for various types of anxiety, and the gender difference in the strength of this relationship is not statistically significant.
The absence of gender differences in the MAachievement link suggests that interventions targeting anxiety may yield similar benefits for women and men in terms of math achievement.
